title: Answers from the Events store arrive day by day

statements.says: Every read Studio makes from the Events store streams its answer back one day at a time, newest day first.
The answer comes as one JSON object per line (NDJSON) over fetch.
The screen shows each day as it lands, so an answer is Arriving until its last day lands and complete after that.
Studio has this one way to load from the Events store.
Health, the telemetry switch and the catalogue stay plain answers.
Making the queries faster stays open as separate work.
A store that stops answering part way keeps the days that landed.
Such an answer ends complete, and where it carries a Gap that Gap is unreachable and names the days it could not read.
Nothing retries by itself.
An answer no screen reads a Gap from ends without one, rather than buy a true Gap with a second query a day.
A screen reads one answer, so it has one Arriving state.
The skills answer carries each day's counts by skill, by trigger and by hour, and the latest Activation.
The activation list and its pages were deleted, so no answer can hit the read cap.
Changing the Filter stops the answer that is arriving.
The treemap on the at-a-glance screen lays itself out again as each day lands, with tiles sliding into place.
The tiles move at once when reduced motion is set.
Health, the telemetry switch and the catalogue read the machine Studio runs on, which is why they stay plain answers.
A 30-day skills answer asks Loki 12 aggregate queries, each about a second over 30 days.
Loki runs 4 queries at a time, so the screen stayed empty for 13 to 15 seconds and passed the API's 5 second limit on a Loki read.
The same 12 queries over the newest single day come back in about half a second.
30 one-day queries cost about the same in total as one 30-day query.
A day-by-day answer puts figures on screen within a second whatever the span, without making the whole answer slower.
An answer built from one query a day counts Activations alone, so its Gap would call a period that only spent quiet.
No screen reads a list of individual events, which is why the activation list was deleted.
Making the queries faster first was not chosen: daily buckets were three times faster on a test Loki split by 24 hours, but the AppHost's Loki splits by 1 hour and was not measured.
Making the queries faster first also lost because a faster total still grows with the span, so a longer span or a busier organisation brings the empty screen back.
Sending one figure at a time was rejected, because counts would land before cost so the figures on screen would cover different things, and the first figure still waits longer as the span grows.
One request per day from the browser was rejected, because a month is 30 requests and the browser would have to order the days and decide what a failure means, which the server decides in one place.

Server-sent events were rejected, because EventSource only sends GET, cannot take the abort signal every read already uses, and reconnects on its own, so a store that stops answering would be retried behind the developer's back.
